For every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is a compact $K'\subset\Omega$ such that a linear map $R:D_0(\Omega)\to D(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ sends tests supported in $K$ to fields supported in $K'$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h$, and is continuous on each fixed-support test space for the seminorms $\sup|\partial^\alpha h|$.

proof_steps.text: For each interval, choose an affine copy of the bump in [A1]. Every derivative on $|s|<1$ is the exponential times a finite sum of rational terms with poles of finite order at $|s|=1$; $e^{-1/(1-s^2)}$ tends to zero faster than every such power, so extension by zero is smooth. Its integral is finite and positive, so normalization gives $\theta_i$. For $d=1$, put $(Rh)(x)=\int_{a_1}^x h(s)\,ds$. Its derivative is $h$, and it vanishes near both endpoints because $h$ is compactly supported and has total integral zero. Its support is compact inside the interval, and its $j$th derivative is $h^{(j-1)}$ for $j\ge1$; the zeroth seminorm is bounded by $(b_1-a_1)\sup|h|$. [given, A1, A2, algebra]

proof_steps.text:
For $d>1$, let $x'=(x_2,\ldots,x_d)$ and $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$. Then $\int H=0$ by [A2]. Assuming the construction in dimension $d-1$, define
$$(Rh)_1=\int_{a_1}^{x_1}\bigl(h(s,x')-\theta_1(s)H(x')\bigr)\,ds,\qquad (Rh)_j=\theta_1(x_1)(R'H)_{j-1}(x')\quad(j\ge2).$$

proof_steps.text: If inputs are supported in fixed compact $K$, each coordinate projection $K_i$ is compactly contained in $(a_i,b_i)$. Choose closed intervals $J_i\Subset(a_i,b_i)$ containing $K_i$ and the support of $\theta_i$; for the first component also include the interval hull of these supports. [F2], applied to successive coordinate blocks, identifies all iterated orders with the same box
integral. In particular, the marginal $H(x')=\int_{a_1}^{b_1}h(s,x')\,ds$ has total integral equal

jointly in the remaining parameters follows from the same bound applied to their differences and

public_sections.Definition: Let $d\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $N\ge1$ be integers. Let $Q_d=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ carry the probability measure obtained by pushing normalized Haar measure on $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ forward under $y\mapsto x=2\pi y$; in coordinates this is $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$. For any componentwise integrable real $q:Q_d\to\mathbb R^N$, considered up to equality almost everywhere, and $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, define its componentwise Fourier coefficient by $\widehat q(k)=\int_{Q_d}q(x)e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)$; this integral is finite because $|e^{ik\cdot x}|=1$ and $q\in L^1$. A finite real trigonometric polynomial is a finite sum $q(x)=\sum_{k\in F}a_ke^{ik\cdot x}$, where $F\subset\mathbb Z^d$ is finite and the coefficients, extended by zero outside $F$, satisfy $a_{-k}=\overline{a_k}$. Such polynomials are integrable and satisfy $\widehat q(-k)=\overline{\widehat q(k)}$. Put $w_k=(1+|k|^2)^{1/2}$. For any $s\in\mathbb R$, define $H^s(Q_d;\mathbb R^N)$ as the completion of finite real trigonometric polynomials in the norm $\|q\|_{H^s}^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}w_k^{2s}|\widehat q(k)|^2$. Identify this completion with the weighted coefficient space subject to conjugate symmetry, using finite symmetric cutoffs, and write $\widehat q(k)$ for its coefficient coordinate. If $s\ge0$, each element has a unique $L^2$ representative, and its coefficient coordinate agrees with the normalized integral formula; for $s<0$ no $L^2$ representative is asserted.

proof_steps.text: Under $x=2\pi y$, normalized measure on $\mathbb T^d$ pushes forward to $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$ on $Q_d$, while $e^{2\pi i k\cdot y}$ becomes $e^{ik\cdot x}$. Thus Fourier coefficients and the componentwise $L^2$ inner product are unchanged by this rescaling. [given, F2, F3, algebra]
proof_steps.claim: Under $x=2\pi y$, normalized measure on $\mathbb T^d$ pushes forward to $(2\pi)^{-d}dx$ on $Q_d$, while $e^{2\pi i k\cdot y}$ becomes $e^{ik\cdot x}$. Thus Fourier coefficients and the componentwise $L^2$ inner product are unchanged by this rescaling.

proof_steps.text: Apply [F4] to each of the $N$ components after this rescaling. The coefficient map identifies scalar $L^2(Q_d)$ isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$; summing the component identities gives the vector-valued coefficient isometry. The Countable Choice hypothesis is exactly [F1]. [given, F1, F4, step 1.1]
proof_steps.claim: Apply [F4] to each of the $N$ components after this rescaling. The coefficient map identifies scalar $L^2(Q_d)$ isometrically with $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d)$; summing the component identities gives the vector-valued coefficient isometry. The Countable Choice hypothesis is exactly [F1].

proof_steps.text: Since $w_k^{2s}>0$, symmetric truncations to $|k|_\infty\le M$ converge in the weighted $\ell^2$ norm by convergence of the defining nonnegative series. The conjugate-symmetry condition is preserved by these cutoffs, so the completion is exactly the real weighted coefficient subspace. For $s\ge0$, $w_k^{2s}\ge1$, hence the coefficient sequence is in $\ell^2$ and [F4] gives its unique $L^2$ representative. For $s<0$ the construction gives only the weighted coefficient completion and makes no $L^2$ claim. [given, F4, step 2.1] ∎

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. Use Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval of absolute time in seconds and $E$ is an oriented three-dimensional Euclidean affine space measured in metres. A Newtonian Cartesian inertial chart consists of this absolute-time coordinate and an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$. Write $I_3$ for the $3\times3$ identity matrix and set $\operatorname{SO}(3):=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3,\ \det Q=1\}$. Inertial-chart changes have the form $t'=t+t_0$, $x'=Qx+vt+a$, where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in metres per second, and $Q\in\operatorname{SO}(3)$ is constant. A frame in this statement means such an adapted chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field. Fix one such chart and a nonempty open spatial coordinate region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. All derivatives below are Cartesian derivatives in this fixed chart; the positive coordinate rescaling defined below is not a change of observer.

For a scalar field $f$, $\nabla_x f=(\partial_{x_1}f,\partial_{x_2}f,\partial_{x_3}f)$.

For a vector field $u=(u_i)$, define $D_xu,D:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, $\operatorname{div}_xu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $\Delta_xu,D_tu:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ by $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$, $D=(D_xu+(D_xu)^{\mathsf T})/2$, $\operatorname{div}_xu=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}u_j$, $(\Delta_xu)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_jx_j}u_i$, and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla_x)u$. The fields $D$ and $\operatorname{div}_xu$ have units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Fix constants $\rho_0>0$, $\mu>0$, $U>0$, $L>0$, and $c>0$, and define $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, $\operatorname{Re}=UL/\nu$, and $\operatorname{Ma}=U/c$. In SI units, $[u]=[U]=[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[x]=[L]=\mathrm m$, $[\rho]=[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[p]=[P(\rho)]=[p_{\mathrm{ref}}]=[\sigma]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[\mu]=\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and $[\Theta]=[X]=[\operatorname{Re}]=[\operatorname{Ma}]=1$; thus the two ratios are dimensionless.

Define the dimensionless coordinates and their domains by
$$\Theta=\frac{Ut}{L},\qquad X=\frac{x}{L},\qquad I^*=\left\{\frac{Ut}{L}:t\in I\right\},\qquad \Omega^*=\left\{\frac{x}{L}:x\in\Omega\right\}.$$
The map $\Phi:I\times\Omega\to I^*\times\Omega^*$, $\Phi(t,x)=(Ut/L,x/L)$, is bijective with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)=(L\Theta/U,LX)$. The corresponding $X$-derivatives are defined by the same component formulas.

In the first, force-free branch, let $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time partial derivatives and continuous first and second spatial partial derivatives, and let the pressure field $p:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with continuous first spatial partial derivatives. $$\sigma=-pI_3+2\mu D,\qquad \rho_0D_tu=\operatorname{div}_x\sigma,\qquad (\operatorname{div}_x\sigma)_i=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}\sigma_{ij},$$
where $\sigma:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is stress, $p$ is the constraint multiplier, not an equation-of-state pressure, and the tension-positive stress convention identifies $\sigma n$ as traction on an outward unit normal $n$. Define $u^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*:I^*\times\Omega^*\to\mathbb R$ by
$$u^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{1}{U}u\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr),\qquad p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{p\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)-p_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\rho_0U^2},$$
for a constant reference pressure $p_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb R$. The scaled fields are dimensionless, $[u^*]=[p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*]=1$, and have respectively the same stated velocity and spatial-pressure regularity. Equivalently, $u(t,x)=Uu^*(\Theta,X)$ and $p(t,x)=p_{\mathrm{ref}}+\rho_0U^2p_{\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Theta,X)$. The governing equations become exactly
$$\partial_\Theta u^*+(u^*\cdot\nabla_X)u^*=-\nabla_Xp_{\mathrm{inc}}^*+\operatorname{Re}^{-1}\Delta_Xu^*,\qquad \operatorname{div}_Xu^*=0.$$

In the separate, unforced barotropic Euler branch, let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ and $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous partial derivatives through total order two, and let $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ have continuous derivatives through order two, with pressure measured in pascals. $$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_x(\rho u)=0,\qquad \rho D_tu+\nabla_xP(\rho)=0,$$

$$\rho^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{\rho\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)}{\rho_0},\qquad u^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{u\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(\Theta,X)\bigr)}{U},\qquad p_{\mathrm{bar}}^*(\Theta,X)=\frac{P\bigl(\rho_0\rho^*(\Theta,X)\bigr)-P(\rho_0)}{\rho_0c^2}.$$

$$g_u^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_u(t,x)}{U},\qquad g_{p,\mathrm{inc}}^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_p(t,x)-p_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\rho_0U^2},\qquad g_\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_\rho(t,x)}{\rho_0},\qquad g_{P,\mathrm{bar}}^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{g_P(t,x)-P(\rho_0)}{\rho_0c^2}.$$

$$m^*(\Phi(t,x))=\frac{m(t,x)}{\rho_0U}=\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))u^*(\Phi(t,x)),$$
where $\rho^*(\Phi(t,x))=1$ in the constant-density branch. Thus $m^*$ is dimensionless. Whenever the integrals exist, total momentum on corresponding spatial regions $A\subseteq\Omega$ and $A^*=A/L$ satisfies
$$\int_A \rho u\,dx=\rho_0UL^3\int_{A^*}\rho^*u^*\,dX.$$
The total momentum has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, as does its scale factor $\rho_0UL^3$.

The coefficient identities do not assert an incompressible or inviscid limit, an error bound, uniqueness, identical solutions for different geometries or rescaled data, or a turbulence threshold. They are conditional predictions of the adopted model formulations and are not experimental observations or proof that either model describes a material.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. $$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\left(\frac{v_*}{v}\right)^{\gamma-1}\exp\left(\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\right),$$
with the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. $$e_{\mathrm{int}}(t,x):=e(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad T(t,x):=(\partial_s e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)),\qquad p_{\mathrm{th}}(t,x):=p_{\mathrm{th}}(\rho(t,x),s(t,x))=-(\partial_v e)(v(t,x),s(t,x)).$$

This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation, restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.
